topic.subject: social
topic.title: Globe: latitudes and longitudes
topic.scope: Equator, heat zones, Prime Meridian, longitude and time, Indian Standard Time

misconceptions.statement: Latitudes are physical lines drawn on the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse map representations with physical reality.
misconceptions.fix: Latitudes are imaginary circular lines used to measure distance from the equator.

probe.question: If you travel to the equator, will you see a line on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, it is a painted line.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's children's ideas in science

misconceptions.statement: Longitudes are parallel to each other like latitudes.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all grid lines behave the same way.
misconceptions.fix: Longitudes converge at the poles and are widest at the equator.

probe.question: Do longitudes stay the same distance apart?

misconceptions.root_belief: a rule from whole numbers works everywhere

misconceptions.statement: The Torrid Zone is hot because it is closer to the sun.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the angle of sunlight with physical distance.
misconceptions.fix: The Torrid Zone receives direct vertical rays of the sun, which concentrate heat.

probe.question: Why is the Torrid Zone hot?
probe.wrong_answer: Because it is physically closer to the sun.

misconceptions.root_belief: bigger or more means more effect

misconceptions.statement: Time is the same everywhere on Earth at the same moment.
misconceptions.why: Daily experience of local time makes it hard to grasp global time zones.
misconceptions.fix: Different longitudes face the sun at different times, causing time differences.

probe.question: If it is noon in London, is it noon in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, noon is the same everywhere.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: Indian Standard Time is based on the Prime Meridian.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the global reference point with local standard time.
misconceptions.fix: IST is based on the 82.5°E longitude passing through Mirzapur.
misconceptions.root_belief: one event has one single cause

misconceptions.statement: The Equator is the line at 90 degrees latitude.
misconceptions.why: Students remember 90° as the 'main' or biggest latitude and link it with the most important line, or confuse the Equator with the poles.
misconceptions.fix: The Equator is 0° latitude, the starting line for measuring latitudes. The poles are at 90° N and 90° S.

probe.question: What is the value of latitude at the Equator?

misconceptions.root_belief: Biggest or most important line has the biggest number

misconceptions.statement: The Equator is the longest of all the parallels, so the Tropic of Cancer is the same length as the Equator.
misconceptions.why: Students see all latitudes as parallel horizontal circles on a flat map and assume equal length.
misconceptions.fix: Parallels get smaller in length towards the poles. The Equator is the longest circle, and at the poles the latitude is just a point.

probe.question: Compare the length of the 60° N parallel with the Equator.
probe.wrong_answer: They are equal in length because both are latitudes.

misconceptions.root_belief: Parallel lines on a map are all equal

misconceptions.statement: The Prime Meridian passes through India because it is the starting line of longitudes.
misconceptions.why: Students link the 'prime' or starting line to their own country or a famous place, instead of Greenwich.
misconceptions.fix: The Prime Meridian is 0° longitude and passes through Greenwich near London, England. It divides the Earth into the Eastern and Western Hemispheres.

probe.question: Through which place does the 0° longitude pass?

misconceptions.root_belief: Starting reference lines pass through one's own country

misconceptions.statement: The Sun's rays heat the whole Earth equally because the Sun is the same distance from everywhere.
misconceptions.why: Students think of the Sun as a uniform heater and ignore the angle at which rays fall on the curved Earth.
misconceptions.fix: Rays fall straight (vertically) near the Equator and slant towards the poles, spreading over a larger area, so heat is less there.

probe.question: Why is it much colder at the poles than at the Equator?
probe.wrong_answer: It is not; the Sun heats all places equally.

misconceptions.root_belief: Sunlight arrives the same way everywhere
misconceptions.source_hint: Research on students' ideas about seasons and Sun's heating

misconceptions.statement: The Frigid Zone is cold because it is far from the Sun's rays and has no sunlight at all.
misconceptions.why: Students equate cold with total absence of sunlight, forgetting that polar regions receive slanting rays and sunlight for part of the year.
misconceptions.fix: The Frigid Zone gets sunlight, but the rays are very slanting, so the heat is low. It lies between the Arctic or Antarctic Circle and the pole.

probe.question: Does the Frigid Zone ever receive sunlight?
probe.wrong_answer: No, it never gets sunlight, so it is cold.

misconceptions.statement: Places east of Greenwich are behind in time, and places to the west are ahead.
misconceptions.why: Students reverse the direction because Greenwich is the 'standard' and they mix up which way the Earth rotates.
misconceptions.fix: The Earth rotates from west to east, so places east see the Sun earlier and are ahead of GMT; places west are behind. India is ahead of GMT by 5 hours 30 minutes.

probe.question: When it is 12 noon at Greenwich, will it be earlier or later than noon in India?
probe.wrong_answer: Earlier than noon, because India is east of Greenwich.

misconceptions.root_belief: East means earlier and west means later
misconceptions.source_hint: Studies on time zone and Earth rotation reasoning

misconceptions.statement: Latitude is always written first or second at will, and a place can be found with only one of its coordinates.
misconceptions.why: Students think one line (latitude or longitude) is enough to name a point, forgetting that each only fixes a whole circle or line.
misconceptions.fix: A place is located where its parallel and meridian cross, so both latitude and longitude are needed in the grid, usually latitude first.

probe.question: Is 20° N latitude enough to tell the exact location of a city?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, 20° N is enough to find the exact city.

misconceptions.root_belief: One coordinate is enough to fix a place
misconceptions.source_hint: Research on students' use of coordinate systems on globes and maps
